doc.title: Phil Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 27, 2023

title: New England Conservatory in 1955 and the humanity of Berklee
summary: Jazz was a dirty word at the Conservatory, in contrast to Berklee's family feeling.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Is the atmosphere at Berklee more like a family? Were you, I’m trying to get this idea about the academic level. Was it less about testing and goals than it was about just learning to play gigs?

You know what made Berklee, to me, was the humanity of the faculty in 1965, ’66, actually go back to ’55. I go back a whole lot more years. But when I went to the New England Conservatory in 1955, jazz was a dirty word. It was the popular department and there were a few of us, like Roger Kellaway, the great pianist, and Freddie Buda, the percussionist for the Pops, great drummer, and myself and a few others, Al Nathan, were into jazz and we just were not interested in going immediately into the symphony. That was their thing. If you were going in for the symphony you were in the right place. But if you were a jazzer you were in the wrong place at that time. It has changed so please forgive me, it’s turned out to be different, a fine top-of-the-line school that it should have always been as far as I’m concerned.
